en: Translated during the Song Dynasty by Guṇabhadra, in accordance with the Imperial Edict.
Recorded by the monk Zongle, Subject and Abbot of the Tianjie Shan-shi Chan Monastery in the Great Ming.

The Abbot of Yanfu Jangsi Temple, the Subject-Monk Ruxi, respectfully received the Imperial Edict to co-comment on the third chapter, "The Essence of the Mind of All Buddhas. Chapter Three. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying:
"I shall now explain the characteristics of the various types of the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*)."
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction.”
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"There are three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*). What are the three?

These are: the mind-made body born of the meditative absorption in the bliss of samādhi, the mind-made body born of the realization of the self-nature of phenomena, and the mind-made body born of the spontaneous manifestation of its class.
The practitioner realizes the marks of progressively superior advancement from the first stage upward and attains the three kinds of bodies.

These three kinds of mind-made bodies constitute the path for Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) to cultivate themselves and transform others; as such, they are essential knowledge for those who are Bodhisattvas. Therefore, the Tathāgata informed them of this without waiting to be asked.
First, three names are listed, followed by their detailed explanation:
"Mahāmati, what is the mind-made body born of the correct meditative absorption in the bliss of samādhi?"

This refers to the samādhi-blissful absorption (*samādhi-sukha-samāpatti*) of the third, fourth, and fifth stages. Because one dwells in the tranquility of the various manifestations of one’s own mind, the marks of consciousness that arise as waves upon the ocean of the mind do not manifest. Knowing that the nature of the objects appearing from one's own mind is neither existent nor non-existent—this is called the "mind-made body born of the blissful absorption of samādhi" (*samādhi-sukha-samāpatti-manomaya-kāya*).

Regarding the "mind-made body born of the meditative absorption in the bliss of samādhi": this bodhisattva, from the third stage through the fourth stage, eliminates the delusions of views; from the fifth stage through the seventh stage, they eliminate the delusions of mental afflictions, thereby attaining the bliss of the samādhi of true emptiness.
"Samādhi" is translated as "correct reception" (*samyag-āpatti*); to speak of it as "samādhi" and also as "correct reception" is to present both the Chinese and the Indic terms together.
As for the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*), it refers to the body of the dharma-nature of true emptiness, which is accomplished through mental attention.

Regarding "the various aspects of one's own mind and so forth": this means that when a bodhisattva realizes emptiness, they differ from those of the two vehicles who give rise to attachment toward mental states and are moved by the winds of signs; therefore, it is said that [the bodhisattva] dwells securely in the ocean of the mind.

Furthermore, it is not like ordinary beings who give rise to the waves of the six consciousnesses; rather, they realize that all objective realms are merely manifestations of one's own mind and are devoid of intrinsic nature.
This constitutes the first chapter on the birth-body (*janmakāya*).
This is the body of self-cultivation. "Mahāmati,
what is the mind-made body that realizes the nature of the self-nature of phenomena?

This refers to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), where one observes and realizes that all phenomena such as illusions are entirely non-existent; the body and mind undergo transformation, and one attains the illusion-like samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*) as well as other gateways of samādhi, immeasurable marks, powers, masteries, and clarities. Adorned like exquisite flowers, moving with swiftness according to one's will—like an illusion, a dream, the moon in water, or a reflection in a mirror—it is neither created nor created from causes, yet it appears as if created and produced from causes. Fully endowed with the various limbs of all forms and adorned, it enters into all Buddha-fields and great assemblies because of its penetration of the self-nature of phenomena; this is called the "mind-made body born of the realization of the self-nature of phenomena" (*dharmasvabhāvagatimati-kāya*).

This means that when a Bodhisattva enters the eighth stage, they realize that all phenomena are like illusions and are devoid of marks; their body and mind undergo a transformation such that they are unimpeded, and they abide in various illusion-like samādhi-doors. They enter universally into Buddha-fields with sovereign supernormal powers, like the adornment of exquisite flowers.
Regarding the swift utterance of words that are "as if like a wish-fulfilling gem" or "like an illusion," these all refer to the unimpeded swiftness of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
As for "neither created nor created from [the elements]," this means that the physical characteristics of the transformation body do not result from the actual creation of the four great elements.

Regarding "the primary elements and their derivatives": this refers to how these material forms resemble their primary causes. Just as these illusory constructed forms are fully adorned with merit and wisdom and manifest their forms throughout the lands, one realizes that all such phenomena are of the nature of one's own self-nature; this is the *svābhāvika-nairmāṇika-kāya* (body born of the nature of self-nature).
This refers to transforming others. "Mahāmati,
what is the body born of mind that is spontaneously produced along with its species and is free from deliberate effort?"

That which is called the realization of all Buddha-dharmas through the mark of self-attained bliss from conditions is termed the "body born of mental attention that is innate and of the same category.
Mahāmati, one should study and train in the observation and realization of the characteristics of these three kinds of bodies.
Initially, one proceeds from the provisional [existence] of saṃsāra into the emptiness of nirvāṇa; subsequently, one proceeds from the emptiness of nirvāṇa into the establishment of the provisional.

These are still the two extremes. Now, one enters the Middle Way, which is called awakening to all Buddha-dharmas and so forth. It is said that from the eighth stage onward, the Bodhisattva enters the stage of dedication (pariṇāmanā), thoroughly comprehending that the dharma-characteristics realized by all Buddhas are none other than one’s own mind; therefore, it is called "attaining the mark of self-joy."
Regarding the phrase "congenital by way of category," the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states:
"To realize the Dharma realized by the Buddha is to immediately enter the Middle Way; this belongs to the category of the Buddha.
Some claim this refers to thousands or tens of thousands of categories, but that is incorrect.
Since one has already entered the Middle Way oneself, the sentient beings to be transformed also belong to the same category as the Buddhas; therefore, it is said that they are "born together.
Upon reaching this stage, wisdom transforms and activity merges, which is termed "non-action" (wu xingzuo).
Before entering the realization of the Way, one is merely termed "mind-born"; this is the third characteristic of the mind-born body.
These three types of bodily characteristics are explained according to their respective stages and positions.
In the second fascicle it says:
"It is like the mind moving with extreme rapidity.
To explain this in terms of both the objective location (*sthāna*) and the vow (*praṇidhāna*), this constitutes a general explanation.
The exhortation to practice and study is as can be seen in the text.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"It is not that I ride the Great Vehicle; It is neither speech nor letters."
Neither truth nor liberation, yet not without a realm;
riding upon the Mahāyāna, with mastery over samādhi,
they possess various mind-made bodies, adorned with the flowers of sovereignty.

The first four lines of the verse concern the Tathāgata’s self-realization as being free from characteristics; therefore, they all employ the term "non-. This means that although it is the Mahāyāna, because it is free from characteristics, there is no vehicle to be mounted.
Indeed, being free from all names and characteristics, there is neither realization nor attainment; yet, it is not that no realm can be demonstrated.

Now, regarding those who "mount the Mahāyāna": "mounting" refers to the act of mounting, while "Mahāyāna" refers to the dharma that is mounted—namely, the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*), which constitute the dharma of the Great Vehicle.
Samādhi refers to the first type of mind-made body (*manomayakāya*).
"Various mind-made [bodies]" refers to the spontaneously born bodies that transcend categories.
"Adorned with flowers" refers to the second type of mind-made body.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has said:"
"If a man or a woman commits the five deeds of immediate retribution, they do not enter the Avīci Hell.
World-Honored One,
how is it that a man or a woman who commits the five deeds of immediate retribution does not enter the Avīci Hell?
The Buddha said to Mahāmati:
"Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for your sake.
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying, "Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"So be it; we shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"What are the five deeds of immediate retribution?"
These are: killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, harming an Arhat, causing schism in the Sangha, and with malicious intent shedding the blood of a Buddha.
These five acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) represent the ultimate in heinousness; whoever commits such deeds will inevitably receive the retribution of the Avīci Hell.
At times the Tathāgata has said that there are those who commit the five acts of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma) yet do not enter the Avīci hell; "Avīci" is synonymous with "immediate.
Mahāmati, not yet having understood this, questioned the Buddha accordingly.
In the response, first the names are listed according to their factual basis, followed by an investigation and explanation based on the Dharma.
Although the names follow a reverse order, the Dharma is in fact strictly sequential; the meaning of this will be seen in the following text. "Mahāmati!..."
What is the mother of sentient beings?

It is craving for renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust; it stands as the basis, like a mother. Ignorance is the father, which gives birth to the village of the sense bases. To sever these two roots is called "killing one's parents."

Craving is the mother and ignorance is the father; this refers to the craving of the present within the twelve links of dependent origination. Arising further from feeling, it coexists with future greed and delight, both of which possess the sense of "birth. Just as a mother nurtures her child, [craving] brings about immediate birth.
Through ignorance and craving, the village of the six sense bases, the twelve sense fields, and so forth arises.
To sever this root of craving and ignorance is the meaning of "killing one's father and mother."
"Those latent tendencies (anuśaya) do not manifest, like the onset of rat-poison; when all dharmas are ultimately severed, that is called 'killing an Arhat'.
Regarding "those latent tendencies do not manifest," it means that the Arhat has already severed the active outbursts (paryavasthāna), yet has not yet severed the residual habit-energies (vāsanā).

It is like a person bitten by a rat: although the wound has healed, it breaks out again upon encountering thunder. This serves as a metaphor for the residual habits (*vāsanā*) of an Arhat; though they do not manifest, they suddenly arise when stirred by the "wind of signs," just as Kāśyapa rose to dance upon hearing the lute.
All dharmas are themselves dharmas that are not defiled by ignorance; if one can exhaustively sever them, that constitutes the meaning of harming an Arhat.
"What is meant by 'breaking the Saṃgha'?"
It refers to the aggregation and accumulation of the various aggregates (skandhas) which possess distinct characteristics; to utterly sever these is called "breaking the Sangha.
Since the term "Sangha" denotes a harmonious assembly, it is here spoken of in terms of the harmony of the five aggregates.
"Different characteristics" refers to form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; "accumulation" refers to the accumulation of the five aggregates within birth and death.
If one can sever these, it is the meaning of "breaking the Sangha."

“Mahāmati! Failing to realize that the seven bodies of consciousness are the manifestation of one’s own mind through the perception of external self-characteristics and common characteristics, and instead using the three gates of liberation and the notion of outflow-free purity to ultimately sever those seven kinds of consciousness—this, Mahāmati, is called ‘maliciously shedding the blood of a Buddha.’”
"If a man or woman commits these acts of immediate retribution (ānantarya), they are called the five ānantaryas, and are also called the 'immediate [errors]' (ānantarya-sama).

Regarding "not studying the external, specific, and general characteristics": this means not knowing that the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena are merely manifestations of one's own mind. Thus, through delusion regarding the eight consciousnesses, one maintains only seven consciousnesses; taking the false awakening of the seventh consciousness as the meaning of Buddhahood, such an error cannot be severed except by the untainted practice of the three liberations.
Although the untainted (anāsrava) is fundamentally wholesome, that which is termed "evil" also accords with the meaning of killing and harming.
To give rise to this mind and, by investigating the object, sever the Buddha of the seven consciousnesses—this is precisely the meaning of shedding the blood of a Buddha.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"Regarding the severance of that body of the eight consciousnesses, one takes the ninth consciousness as the Buddha-consciousness and the eight consciousnesses as the Bodhisattva-consciousness, because their substance belongs to ignorance; these are the five internal *ānantarya* [sins]."
From the passage beginning with "As for the man himself" onwards,
it is a general conclusion. Furthermore, Mahāmati,
there is an external uninterrupted [hell], which I shall now explain.
After you and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have heard this meaning, you shall not fall into delusion in future ages.
What are the five *ānantarya*?
They are the *ānantarya* previously mentioned; if one practices these, one will not attain the dharmas of immediate realization (*ānantarya-samādhi*) regarding each of the three gates of liberation.

Apart from these, there are other manifestations of transformative power that appear as the immediate [retribution] (ānantarya), namely: the transformative power of the śrāvaka, the transformative power of the bodhisattva, and the transformative power of the Tathāgata. These manifest as the immediate retribution for the sake of others who have committed an immediate offense, in order to eliminate their doubts and regrets and to inspire them; thus, through the transformations of supernormal power, they appear as the immediate retribution.

There is no one who, while performing deeds of immediate retribution, fails to attain the realization of the immediacy [of liberation], provided they awaken to the fact that all is merely the manifestation of their own mind, abandon the false imaginings regarding the body and possessions, relinquish the grasping for "I" and "mine," and occasionally encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who liberates them from the false imaginings of continuity in other realms of existence.

Regarding "external immediate [retribution]": "external" is contrasted with "internal," referring here to the five internal immediate [sins] as internal, while actually committing an immediate karmic act constitutes the external.

The preceding section explained that by practicing the five acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), one attains the realization of noble wisdom; fearing that people might think that even if one actually creates the causes for such immediate retribution, one would not suffer the evil karmic consequences, he therefore speaks this further.

If one hears that the retribution for the five external acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) does not fail to manifest, then no doubt or confusion arises; therefore, it is said that "one does not fall into folly.

As for the phrase "what was previously taught," this refers to what was once stated in other teachings regarding the immediate [sins]: "If one commits these acts of immediate retribution, one will certainly fall into the Avīci hell; how then could one attain the three kinds of liberation or the dharmas of the immediate [attainment]?"
Below this, regarding the statement "provisionally created": the provisional must lead to the real. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"Seeing those who commit the karma of immediate retribution, [the Buddha], wishing to exhort and inspire them to reform their ways, uses his supernatural powers to manifest as if participating in those very acts; they then immediately repent and eliminate [their transgressions], realizing liberation—this is what is meant by 'walking upon non-paths while penetrating the Buddha-path.'"
"Such as Devadatta, King Ajātaśatru, and others.
The phrase "there are none" means that there is no one who actually commits [an offense] and yet does not receive the retribution of the *ānantarya* (immediate) hell.

However, those who actually commit such acts are not necessarily forever deprived of the three gates of liberation; therefore, it is said that "except for those who have realized that all things are merely the manifestation of one's own mind.

This means that if one can understand that all phenomena are mind-only—neither perceiving a body internally nor perceiving external wealth—and thus remain free from the attachments to persons and dharmas, then even if they are born in other realms in future lives, they will encounter spiritual friends and, by leaving behind the faults of discrimination, attain liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Craving is called the mother; Ignorance is the father.
Consciousness that awakens to objects is the Buddha; The various proclivities are the Arhats.”
"The accumulation of the aggregates (skandhas) is called the Saṃgha;
to sever them in immediate succession is what is meant by the five acts of immediate retribution (ānantarya), whereby one does not enter the Avīci Hell.
This verse refers to the aforementioned five internal acts of immediate retribution.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
I pray that you will explain for us the Buddha’s knowledge and awakening.”
“World-Honored One!
What is the Buddha’s knowledge and awakening?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"To realize the selflessness of persons and phenomena, to fully understand the two obstacles, to be free from the two kinds of death, and to sever the two afflictions—this is called the awakening of a Buddha.
If Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas attain this Dharma, they too are called Buddhas."
"For these reasons, I speak of the One Vehicle.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Thoroughly knowing the two kinds of non-self, The two obstructions and the afflictions are severed."
"Forever free from the two kinds of death—this is called the Buddha’s knowledge and awakening.
The aforementioned discourse on the path of awakening of the One Vehicle was still somewhat brief; it had not yet specified what dharma is known and what is awakened to.
Thereupon, he renewed this request, and the Buddha then addressed him:

"To realize the two kinds of non-self is awakening; to realize the two hindrances is knowledge. Upon thorough investigation, one finds that persons and dharmas, as well as sentient beings and Buddhas, are equal, for fundamentally there are no two attachments."
What is called the realm of True Suchness (tathatā) is beyond birth; "Buddha" is a mere provisional designation, and thus there is no grasping at a person (pudgala-grāha).
Within the state of equality, there are no forms of self or other; thus, there is no grasping at phenomena (dharma-grāha).

Sentient beings are deluded by this and give rise to the two types of self-grasping; the Tathāgata, having realized the fundamental nature, sees that both forms of grasping are empty, and thus it is said that there is no self.
As for the "two obstacles," they are the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Thus, the two aforementioned attachments are taken as the afflictive hindrances and the two emptinesses as wisdom. Since the two emptinesses empty those two attachments, there is no afflictive hindrance;
since the wisdom that is capable of emptying them also vanishes, there is no cognitive hindrance.
The two obstacles are the cause of birth and death; because the cause is extinguished, the effect is extinguished, and thus it is said that one is "freed from the two kinds of death.
These two deaths are the death of fragmentation (*pariccheda*) and the death of transformation (*pariṇāma*).

The two types of afflictions refer to the general and specific delusions; these two categories of delusion must be accumulated until they reach their ultimate limit before they can be completely severed.
To realize and penetrate this in such a manner is called the awakening of a Buddha.

Although the followers of the two vehicles are inferior, if they can turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle and awaken as the Buddha does, they are nothing other than Buddhas; therefore, it is said, "They are also called Buddhas."
This is why the One Vehicle is taught;
the verse of repetition may be consulted.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason has the World-Honored One proclaimed these words among the great assembly:
‘I am all the Buddhas of the past, as well as those who underwent various births’?”
At that time, I was the Cakravartin King Mandhātṛ, the six-tusked great elephant, the parrot, Śakra Devānām Indra, and the seer Sunetra.
"Thus it is taught in the *Śatasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and other scriptures.
While the Way of the Buddhas of the three periods of time is no different, there is nonetheless a distinction between past, future, and present in terms of their sequential awakening."
"How is it that the World-Honored One says, 'I am all the Buddhas of the past,' yet also says,
'In various births, their forms differ'? Mahāmati,
holding these two points, he raises them as a question."
The *Jātaka-nidāna-sūtra* states:

"In the past, the Tathāgata underwent various births, such as those as a universal monarch (cakravartin), Śakra, the great elephant Sunetra, a parrot, and so forth, numbering in the hundreds of thousands."
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Because of the fourfold equality, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha proclaims these words among the great assembly:
'In that time, I was Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa Buddha.'"
"What are the four equalities?
They are equality of letters, equality of speech, equality of dharmas, and equality of body; these are called the four equalities.
Because of these four kinds of equality, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims these words amidst the great assembly."

The Buddha told him that it was because of the fourfold equality (*catuḥ-samatā*) that he became Buddhas such as Krakucchanda; thus he answered the aforementioned question, "I am those Buddhas of the past.
The meaning of the fourfold equality is found in the following section.
"What is the equality of syllables?
If the syllables that designate me as a Buddha are the same syllables that designate all Buddhas, and if those syllables have no difference in their intrinsic nature, this is the equality of names."
What is meant by "equality of speech"?

It refers to the manifestation of my sixty-four kinds of Brahma-voice linguistic qualities; those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are likewise, manifesting sixty-four kinds of Brahma-voice linguistic qualities without increase or decrease, without distinction, possessing the nature of the Brahma-voice of the kalaviṅka bird.
What is meant by "equality of body" (*kāya-samatā*)?

It means that there is no difference between all *ātman*s and the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* and *rūpakāya*, including its marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). Except for the manifestation of various distinct *rūpakāya*s in order to discipline sentient beings of various different realms of existence (*gati*), this is called equality of body.
What is the equality of dharmas?
It refers to both myself and those Buddhas attaining the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; briefly stated, this is the unobstructed wisdom of the Buddha-dharmas.
These are called the four equalities.
"Therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims these words in the midst of the great assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, and Kanakamuni are I."
"By means of these four kinds of equality, I have taught them for the sake of the Buddha's sons.
Regarding the "four equalities," it means that the four—namely, syllables, speech, body, and Dharma—are all equal.
Regarding "equality of name": it means that my name is Buddha, and all Tathāgatas are also named Buddha; since the name "Buddha" is no different, this is called equality of name.
Regarding "equality of speech": it means that I produce speech in sixty-four kinds of Brahma-sounds, and all Buddhas do likewise; this is called equality of speech.

The second chapter of the *Guhyakapūrvayoga-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Secret-Trace Malla) states that the Buddha’s voice possesses eight grammatical cases (*vibhakti*), namely: substance (*svabhāva*), action (*karman*), instrument (*karaṇa*), purpose (*sampradāna*), origin (*apādāna*), relation (*sambandha*), location (*adhikaraṇa*), and vocative (*āmantraṇa*). Each of these eight cases possesses eight qualities: the harmonious voice, the gentle voice, the distinct voice, the easily understood voice, the unerring voice, the non-feminine/non-petulant voice, the vast voice, and the deep-reaching voice. These eight sets of eight constitute sixty-four kinds of vocal quality.
*Kiṃnara* is the name of a bird whose voice is pure and elegant, surpassing that of all other birds; therefore, it is cited here as a metaphor.

Regarding "the bodies are equal," this means that my body and the *dharmakāya*, *saṃbhogakāya*, and *nirmāṇakāya* of the Buddhas are equal and without distinction. Although the capacities of sentient beings are not equal and the manifested traces may differ, when their ultimate destination is realized, they are one and the same.
"Equality of dharmas" means that the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) attained are no different from those of all Buddhas.

"Unobstructed wisdom" means that by attaining these four equalities, one encounters no obstacles regarding any of the Buddha-dharmas, nor is one confused about the similarities and differences in the traces of the Tathāgata’s transformations.
Mahāmati spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
"As the World-Honored One has said:

'From the night I attained supreme perfect enlightenment until the night I enter parinirvāṇa, in the interval between these two times, not even a single word has been spoken; nor have I spoken, nor shall I speak. That which is not spoken is what is called the teaching of the Buddha.'"
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha say that what is not spoken is the word of the Buddha?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"I speak thus because of two dharmas. What are these two dharmas?
They are the dharma realized by oneself and the dharma that has existed from the beginning; these are called the two dharmas."
"It is because of these two dharmas that I speak thus.
Since the demonstration of the fourfold equality still involves verbal expression, he further asks about the meaning of not having spoken a single word from beginning to end.
The Buddha answered that it is because of two dharmas: namely, that there is no dharma that can be spoken—this is the teaching of the Buddha.

"Self-attainment" refers to the merit of self-realization through cultivation; "original abiding" refers to the inherent merit of the nature. Since cultivation and nature are identical and both transcend verbal expression, he said, "I speak thus."
"What is meant by 'the dharma realized through one's own attainment'?

It is that which the Tathāgata has attained, and which I too have attained—without increase and without decrease. This is the ultimate realm of the dharma realized through one's own attainment, free from verbal conceptualization and free from the two courses of letters."

It is said that the realm of one's own realization is ultimately no different from that of all Buddhas; since this wondrous state attained by oneself is beyond increase or decrease, how could it ever be accessible to speech or thought?
Therefore it is said: "Transcending verbal expression," and so forth.
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:
"It is free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of conceptual discrimination, and free from the characteristics of names."
Regarding this mention of "two destinies," the details are not yet clear.
What is meant by the "primordially abiding dharma"?
It refers to the ancient path of the sages, which is like the nature of gold, silver, and so forth—permanently abiding within the *dharmadhātu*.
Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the dharma-realm remains eternally constant, like the road leading to that city.

For example, it is like a man traveling through a vast wilderness who sees a level, direct path leading toward an ancient city; he then follows it into the city and experiences bliss according to his wishes.
"Mahāmati, what do you think?
Is it they who create this path and the various pleasures within the city?"
He replied, "No. The Buddha said to Mahāmati:
“Both myself and all the Buddhas of the past, as well as the eternally abiding Dharma-realm, are likewise thus.

Therefore it is said: ‘From the night I attained supreme perfect enlightenment until the night I entered parinirvāṇa, not a single word was spoken between them; nor has anything been spoken, nor will anything be spoken.’”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"From the night I attained enlightenment until the night of my parinirvāṇa,
in the interval between these two, I have not spoken a single word."
"Because I abide in the Dharma realized by myself, I have made this statement:
'That Buddha and I are entirely without distinction.
What is called "the path of the ancient sages" refers precisely to the Dharma of inherent virtue realized by the Buddhas of the past.

Regarding the nature of gold, silver, and so forth: this is a metaphor for the primordially abiding *dharmatā*, which is like the hardness and strength of gold, not something obtained through smelting or refinement.
The permanence of the *dharmadhātu* is likewise; that is to say, whether a Buddha appears or not, its intrinsic nature and characteristics abide eternally.
Furthermore, the statement that "the dharma-realm is eternally abiding" concludes the discussion on the primordially abiding dharma (*prakṛtistha-dharma*).

Moreover, the phrase "like the path leading to that city" and so forth serves as a combined metaphor for the fact that both the self-attained dharma and the primordially abiding dharma ultimately converge into a single consistency.
That which is called the level and correct path is the Dharma of primordial abiding;
the man entering the city and experiencing joy is the Dharma of self-attainment.
Because he possesses the original correct path, he is able to follow it and enter; having entered, he rests therein—all of this is not an external thing.

It is said that the inherent nature of these two dharmas transcends the reach of speech and thought; thus, although not a single word was spoken throughout the Great Canon of teachings over fifty years, this does not mean there was nothing taught. Rather, it was by means of words dispelling words, for the ultimate aim of all Buddhas of the three periods of time is one and the same.
The verses are clear in their meaning and are not further explained.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again requested:
"World-Honored One!

I only pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of existence and non-existence regarding all dharmas, so that I and other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may be free from the characteristics of existence and non-existence and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati:
"Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for your sake.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"Indeed, we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"There are two kinds of dependence in this world:"
This means that based on existence and non-existence, one falls into the categories of being and non-being, desiring to see [reality] while failing to depart from the characteristics of departure.

The ultimate truth is quiescent and absolute, being neither existent nor non-existent; sentient beings are deluded regarding this and fall into the two extremes, unable to return to their original state. Therefore, Mahāmati raises questions for the sake of the assembly.
The Buddha first answers by following the question, and subsequently probes and explains its meaning.
Regarding "relying on the two kinds [of objects]," this means that worldly sentient beings give rise to views of existence and non-existence based on the objects of existence and non-existence.
To fall into the view of existence and non-existence is precisely the view of being and non-being.
To "desire to see" means to take pleasure in and become attached to this view.
Because one falsely claims that which is not the Dharma of transcendence to be transcendence, it is said that one does not depart from the characteristic of departing.
“Mahāmati! What is meant by the world depending on existence?
It means that the world arises from causes and conditions; it is not non-existent.”
Arising exists; it is not that arising does not exist.
Mahāmati, those who speak in such a manner are asserting that the world is without cause.
Mahāmati! What is meant by the worldly reliance on non-existence?

It refers to having first experienced the nature of greed, anger, and delusion, and subsequently engaging in false conceptualization and attachment regarding whether that nature of greed, anger, and delusion exists or does not exist.

Mahāmati! If one does not grasp at the existence of intrinsic nature, it is because the characteristics of such a nature are quiescent; that is to say, the Tathāgatas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas do not grasp the nature of greed, anger, and delusion as being either existent or non-existent.

The phrase "depending on existence" (*bhava*) below explains the characteristic of existence: it means that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions that truly exist; they do not lack reality, for they truly arise from existence.

To say that it is not the case that there is no arising means that the causes and conditions capable of producing [arising] do exist; because this reckons what is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as being conditioned, he further declares:
"Those who speak thus belong to the causeless theories (*ahetuvāda*) of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*)."

"Based on the absence of a lower [state]" explains "signlessness": this means that after first having accepted the nature of the three poisons, one subsequently falsely conceptualizes that nature as being non-existent; this non-existence is precisely what is falsely conceptualized as "nothingness."
If one does not falsely accept the three poisons as having an intrinsic nature, then there is nothing to be grasped.

When there is no grasping, their nature and characteristics are primordially quiescent; this is like the Buddhas and those of the Two Vehicles who do not grasp at the nature of the three poisons, thereby departing from the views of existence and non-existence.
“Mahāmati, what herein is meant by ‘one who destroys’?
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If one grasps the nature of greed, anger, and delusion, one will not grasp them again later.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Excellent! Excellent! You have understood it thus."

Mahāmati! It is not only that the nature of greed, anger, and delusion—whether as existent or non-existent—is a destroyer; it is also a destroyer of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and even the Buddhas. Why is this so?
"This is because both the internal and external are unapprehendable, and because the nature of afflictions is neither different nor non-different.

Having thus explained the characteristics of existence and non-existence in response to Mahāmati’s request, the Tathāgata then asked about these two questions: "Who are those who destroy the Buddha-dharma?"
Mahāmati then replied that for one who first takes the nature of the three poisons to be existent and later reckons it to be non-existent is the meaning of "destruction.
The Buddha affirmed his statement, saying, "It is not only the reckoning of non-existence that constitutes destruction; it also destroys the two vehicles and the Buddha."

It is because they claim that the Buddha and those of the two vehicles also originally took the three poisons to be existent, and later, by eliminating the three poisons, took them to be non-existent, thereby attaining the fruit of sainthood; thus, they say that [the Buddha] is also a destroyer.

Why is this so? It means that the Noble Ones have thoroughly realized that all internal and external phenomena are unattainable, and they have also realized that the nature of afflictions is fundamentally free from the four extremes, such as identity and difference; how then could there be anything to be destroyed?

“Mahāmati! Greed, hatred, and delusion—whether internal or external—cannot be apprehended. Because the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion has no body and no grasping, it is not the Buddhas, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas who destroy them.”
Because Buddhas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas are liberated by their very nature, bondage and the causes of bondage do not exist as intrinsic realities.
Mahāmati! If there were one who was bound, then there would have to be bondage, because that [bound person] would be the cause of bondage.
"Mahāmati! Such talk of 'destruction' is called the characteristic of non-existence.
Following the discussion on greed, hatred, and delusion, he further explains the reason why [the Tathāgata] is indestructible.
Regarding the statement "whether internal or external," it means that the nature of the three poisons cannot be found when sought within, without, or in between.
Since they cannot be found, how could there be any essential nature to be grasped?
Therefore, the conclusion states: "It is not the Buddha, the śrāvakas, or the pratyekabuddhas who are the destroyers.
This is because the nature of the Buddha and the two vehicles is liberation by its very essence; it is neither bound nor liberated.

Furthermore, it is said that if there is one who is bound, this means that having previously experienced [suffering], they do not subsequently take it up; thus, there is already bondage. Bondage is its fruit, and since every fruit must have a cause, the cause is precisely craving and so forth.
Where there is bondage, there is destruction; to speak thus of destruction is to fall into the nihilistic view of emptiness. Therefore, it is said that "there is no characteristic. "Mahāmati!..."

For this reason, Mahāmati, I say that it would be better to hold a view of a personal self as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to a view of emptiness based on the overweening pride of non-existence.

Mahāmati, those who possess the overweening pride of non-existence are called "ruiners. They fall into the expectations of views regarding individual and common characteristics; they do not understand that all is a manifestation of one's own mind. Seeing external natures as impermanent, perishing moment by moment, and observing the continuous flow and transformation of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, they abandon the conceptualization of verbal signs. Such people are called "ruiners."

It is better to take the "view of persons" (pudgala-dṛṣṭi) as inferior, using the great to illustrate the small, thereby clarifying the error of the view of emptiness; for the "view of persons" is precisely the "view of self" (ātma-dṛṣṭi).
As for the term "arrogance of overestimation" (adhimāna), it refers to the superiority of one's own dharmas, which results in the pride of such a view.
The Sūtra says:
"To claim what has not been attained as attained, and to claim what has not been realized as realized"—
this refers precisely to such a person.

The evil resulting from the view of a person (*pudgaladṛṣṭi*) is limited; however, when one holds the empty view of overweening pride (*abhimāna*), there is no dharma that is not abandoned—this is what is called "ruination.
Therefore it is said: "It is better to give rise to the view of a person as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to the view of emptiness."

Falling into views of self-origination and co-origination, etc., explains the cause for giving rise to the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*). This is truly because, since beginningless time, one has given rise to views of self-arising and co-arising, taking pleasure and desire therein; failing to understand that all phenomena are mind-only, one perceives external phenomena as arising and ceasing moment by moment, undergoing successive transformation and decay—namely, the continuous flow and transformation of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)—and reckons that these real dharmas, once destroyed, return to nothingness. This is the view of emptiness.
Regarding the meaning of arising and ceasing even within false discrimination that is free from the characteristics of words:
at that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Existence and non-existence are two extremes, up to the sphere of the mind."
Purifying those objects of perception, the mind of equanimity is stilled.
Without grasping at the nature of objects, cessation is not a state of nothingness;
all phenomena are suchness, like the sphere of the noble ones.
Arising without seeds, having arisen they again perish;
that which exists through causes and conditions yet is not truly existent does not abide within my teaching.
It is neither of the non-Buddhists nor of the Buddha; it is neither mine nor anyone else’s.
Arising from the gathering of causes and conditions, how could it be non-existent?
Who asserts that what exists through the gathering of causes and conditions is then said to be non-existent?
Such proponents of false views discourse on arising and ceasing, delusively conceptualizing existence and non-existence.
"If one knows that there is nothing produced, And likewise nothing extinguished,
Observing all this as entirely empty and quiescent, One is free from both existence and non-existence.
The first eight lines praise the correct meaning of the Inner Teachings (Buddhism).
To claim that something arises from no cause and yet exists is a false conceptualization regarding arising and ceasing, existence and non-existence;

it is not my teaching. This is not among the four positions of the non-Buddhists and others. The Buddha said: "Whatever phenomena of arising I have taught were not created by a Buddha, nor by non-Buddhists, nor produced by a divine self (*puruṣa*), nor fashioned by any other cause. Rather, they arise through the gathering together of the harmony of primary causes and conditions. Nevertheless, with respect to what has arisen, one cannot say it is non-existent."

Regarding the phrase "who assembles the causes and conditions," it means that among the dharmas produced by primary causes and conditions, neither a self nor anything graspable can be found; who, then, could exist and who could not?
As for what is discussed by those with false views, this is merely a deluded calculation of existence, non-existence, arising, and ceasing.

If one knows that birth is fundamentally non-arising and cessation is likewise non-cessation, naturally and wondrously accords with emptiness and stillness, and does not fall into the two views of existence and non-existence; therefore, it is said: "One is detached from both existence and non-existence."
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that you will explain for me and for all bodhisattvas the characteristics of the penetration of the fundamental principle.”
If one can skillfully discern the characteristics of the penetration of the ultimate truth (*siddhānta*), I and all bodhisattvas have realized these characteristics.
Having realized these characteristics, one will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and will not follow after discursive perceptions or the various māras and non-Buddhist paths.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!”
"Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "So be it;
I shall receive your instruction."
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas have two kinds of general characteristics, namely, the penetration of the fundamental principle (zongtong) and the penetration of the teaching (shuotong)."
"To skillfully transform and guide others, one must master both the essence and the exposition; only then can one lead beings to the Way.
For the essence is the foundation of the Way, while the exposition is the trace of the teaching."
The school (zong) serves to clarify the ultimate goal; if the goal is not clarified, one loses the destination to which one should return.
The teaching (jiao) serves to explicate the principle; if the principle is obscured, one becomes lost regarding the path by which to enter.
Therefore, when the school is realized but the teaching is not mastered, the principle remains subtle yet unmanifest.
If the doctrine is communicated while the essential principle is not, the words may be eloquent yet lack substance.
These two, however, truly require one another for their function and must not be neglected in isolation.

When Mahāmati requested an explanation of the characteristics of the penetration of the essential principle (*zongtong*) but did not mention the penetration of the teaching (*shuotong*), he was merely citing its core; once the penetration of the essential principle is established, the penetration of the teaching is inherently contained within it.
In the response, the mention of both [aspects] is because they must be twofold before being complete. "Mahāmati!

As for the penetration of the essence (zongtong), it refers to the characteristics of supreme advancement attained through personal realization; it is far removed from the delusions of speech, words, and letters; it proceeds toward the outflow-free realm (anāsrava-dhātu) and the self-characteristics of the stage of self-realization; it is far removed from all false and illusory perceptions; and it subdues all externalists and māras."
"The radiance of the light of self-realization is what is called the characteristic of the ultimate principle (zōngtōng).

The ultimate principle refers to the characteristic of one's own supreme realization; it means that by relying on the teachings to contemplate and practice, one attains the meaning while forgetting the words, transcends the discrimination of letters and texts, enters the stages and abodes, awakens to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), surpasses the realized wisdom of the three vehicles, naturally subdues demons and heterodoxies, and reaches the stage of Buddhahood. When the ultimate awakened wisdom shines forth alone and brilliantly, this is the characteristic of the ultimate limit of the ultimate principle."
"What is the characteristic of the penetration of teaching?

It refers to the teaching of the various doctrines of the ninefold canon, which is free from characteristics such as difference and non-difference, existence and non-existence, and so forth. By employing skillful means to accord with sentient beings, one preaches the Dharma as appropriate, enabling them to attain liberation; this is called the characteristic of the penetration of teaching."
"Mahāmati! You and the other bodhisattvas should practice and study this.

As for the characteristics of the communication of the teaching (deśanā-pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa), it refers to the characteristics of expounding the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.

The "ninefold division" refers to nine of the twelve divisions [of the scriptures]; however, there are differences between the Great and Small Vehicles. If one speaks of the ninefold division of the Hīnayāna, it lacks three sections: the Vaipulya (Extensive), the *Aparapṛṣṭājñapti* (Unasked Spontaneous Teaching), and the Vyākaraṇa (Prophecy).
As the sutra says:
"These ninefold teachings of mine are spoken in accordance with sentient beings.

If one refers to the ninefold division of the Mahayana, it lacks the three categories of nidāna (causes and conditions), avadāna (parables), and upadeśa (exegesis), as stated in the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra).
This is an answer given according to specific distinctions; in general discourse, there are twelve divisions, also called the twelvefold teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-dharma-pravacana*).

Here, although nine divisions are mentioned, since it is said that they are taught according to the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) for the sake of sentient beings, this represents the process of entering the Great Vehicle from the Small Vehicle.

Regarding the statement that one is "free from difference and non-difference, existence and non-existence," this means that once one has transcended the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), there is no hindrance to the fourfold teaching.

Furthermore, as for the phrase "preaching the Dharma as is appropriate," "appropriate" (*yathāyogam*) means "as it ought to be. To say "one should preach by means of which dharma" refers to preaching accordingly so that sentient beings may attain liberation.
This is the characteristic of the commonality taught subsequent to the fruit of the Tathāgata; it is something that those who are bodhisattvas must certainly study.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The characteristics of the commonality of the fundamental doctrine and its teaching, The conditions, the self-nature, and the teaching of the Dharma."
"Seeing well and discerning well, one does not follow various conceptualizations.
The first three lines of this verse describe the characteristics of the two types of penetration.
"Seeing well" refers to the penetration of the essence (zongtong).
"Differentiation" refers to the teaching of the common vehicle.

"Not following various perceptions and conceptions" means that once one attains the characteristics of the two supernormal powers, one no longer follows the forceful perceptions and deluded imaginings of the non-Buddhists.
“Since there is no such thing as true reality, how can the deluded thoughts of fools arise?
The absence of intrinsic nature is liberation.”
If one gives rise to conceptual discrimination regarding the true nature of suchness without having attained it, it is no different from the deluded imaginings of ordinary people.
What is meant by "deluded imagining"?
It is the false reckoning that the non-existence of all phenomena constitutes liberation.
Non-nature is precisely non-existence.
"Observing all conditioned phenomena, Which continue in a succession of arising and ceasing,
One increases the two views, Being inverted and lacking true knowledge."
"The first is the True Reality; freedom from transgression is Nirvana.
Contemplate the delusions of the world as being like illusions, dreams, and plantain trees.

The Tathāgata, with the eye of correct wisdom, contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in the world as being entirely illusory, subject to arising and ceasing, yet falsely reckoned as real, thereby increasing the two views of existence and non-existence. Ordinary fools are inverted and lack any true awakening; apart from the single, wondrous mind of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and Nirvana, everything else is false and deceptive. Therefore, they are metaphorically described as "like illusions, dreams, and plantain trees."
To be "without fault" means to realize that the nature of faults is fundamentally empty; this is itself nirvāṇa.
"Though there be greed, anger, and delusion, In truth, there is no person at all.
From craving arise the aggregates; All that exists is like a phantom or a dream."
This is a further explanation of the meaning of "like an illusion" and so forth.
Although it is said that there are the three poisons, there is no person who can give rise to them; for since the two kinds of self are fundamentally empty, how could the three poisons exist?
"This means that the capacity to generate craving and the five aggregates thus produced are both like dreams and illusions.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
I only pray that you will explain the characteristics of unreal conceptualization.
How does unreal conceptualization arise?
What kind of phenomena are called unreal conceptualization?
"In regard to which phenomena do unreal imaginings arise?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Excellent!"
Excellent! You have been able to ask the Tathāgata about such a meaning; it will bring great benefit and great peace and happiness, out of compassion for all devas and humans in the world.
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well; I shall speak for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction.”
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Mahāmati,
various kinds of unreal conceptualizations and attachments to various meanings give rise to discrimination."

Attached to the grasped and the grasper, they do not understand that these are merely the manifestations of their own minds; falling into the views of existence and non-existence, they increase the views of the heterodox.
Clinging to various external objects through the habitual tendencies of false imagination, the mind and its mental factors give rise to the false imagination of "self" and "what belongs to self."
One who exhausts delusive thoughts must reach their ultimate limit; one who reveals the true nature must exhaust its source.
When the source is exhausted, the true nature is naturally manifest; when the limit is reached, where can delusive thoughts exist?
Therefore, Mahāmati inquired about the characteristics of unreal conceptualization (abhūta-parikalpa), posing three questions in total:
first, he asked how conceptualization arises;
second, he asked what dharma is termed conceptualization.
The third question asks from what do deluded thoughts arise?
The Buddha answers in sequence to explain this.

Regarding the first answer concerning "various meanings" (*nānārtha*): in all external phenomena there are various characteristics; these meanings are entirely false and arise based upon them. Therefore, various unreal deluded thoughts and attachments arise.

Next, the response regarding "clinging to the grasped and the grasper" refers to clinging to the sense organs and their objects while failing to realize they are manifestations of mind-only, as well as falling into views of existence or non-existence outside of the mind. Based on these, the various views of the externalists increase; all such views are illusory dharmas. By knowing these dharmas, one knows why they are illusory.
The subsequent response regarding "the habitual tendencies of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa-vāsanā*) and so forth" refers precisely to that which serves as the basis.

Furthermore, when it says, "It arises from the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) clinging through deluded conceptualization to 'self' and 'what belongs to self' (*ātma-ātmīya*)," this means that the two types of self—the person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*)—are its locus. Once one knows this locus, one knows the source from which delusion arises; since the source is not real, delusion is extinguished.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
if various kinds of meanings and various kinds of unreal conceptual attachments give rise to false discrimination, [how is it so?]”

Through attachment to the grasped and the grasper, one fails to understand that [the world] is merely the manifestation of one's own mind and falls into the views of existence and non-existence, thereby increasing the views of the non-Buddhists.

Through attachment to various external objects due to the habitual tendencies of false imagination (*vikalpa-vāsanā*), there arises attachment to a self and what belongs to a self (*ātma-ātmīya*) within the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitasika*).
World-Honored One!
If such various external characteristics of objects fall into the marks of existence and non-existence, yet are free from being and non-being, and free from the marks of views—
World-Honored One!

The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is likewise so: it is free from the characteristics of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), sense organs (*indriya*), parts (*avayava*), analogies (*dṛṣṭānta*), and logical reasons (*hetu*).

World-Honored One, for what reason does false discrimination (*vikalpa*) regarding the unreal meaning of a single locus give rise to various attachments to natures, whereas false discrimination regarding the characteristics of the locus of the ultimate truth does not give rise to such attachments?
"Could it be that the World-Honored One is teaching a doctrine of false causes,
asserting that some things arise while others do not?
Having spoken thus, Mahāmati reiterated the meaning of what had been said above to pose his subsequent question.

My intention is this: if the Buddha speaks in such a manner, then even those various external objects that fall into the characteristics of existence and non-existence are, by their very nature, free from existence and non-existence and free from the characteristics of all views.

However, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is likewise free from the characteristics of the sense faculties, means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Since the various external objects are no different from the ultimate truth, for what reason do you say that various objects give rise to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) while the ultimate truth does not?
"Is it not the case that what the World-Honored One has said contradicts reason—that there is both arising and non-arising?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"It is not that through false discrimination there is one kind of arising and another kind of non-arising."

Why is this so? Because false discriminations regarding existence and non-existence do not arise; when one perceives that external appearances are neither existent nor non-existent, and realizes them to be merely the manifestation of one's own mind, false discriminations do not arise.

Mahāmati! I have taught that because of the various marks of false conceptualization within the minds of other ignorant people, their activities appear before them, and thus attachment to the nature and characteristics of those various false conceptualizations arises.

How does a fool come to be free from the views that cling to "I" and "mine," free from the errors regarding agent, action, and causal conditions, and awaken to the measure of his own mind’s false imaginings? Through the transformation of body and mind, he ultimately attains clear understanding of the realm of self-realization of all Tathāgatas across all stages, becoming free from the false imaginings regarding the five dharmas, the self-natures, and the perception of objective phenomena.

For this reason, I say that false discrimination arises from attachment to various unreal objects; by knowing the reality as it is, one attains liberation from the various false discriminations of one's own mind.

The Buddha replied: "I do not falsely discriminate that there is arising in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) nor non-arising in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Therefore, he asks a further question to explain why there is arising and non-arising.

This means that by comprehending the false imaginings of existence and non-existence, one sees that external dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature; by awakening to the fact that all is a manifestation of mind alone, false imaginings no longer arise. It is not that there is some separate ultimate truth apart from this."

It is only because foolish people do not understand that which is manifested by their own minds that they perceive the conditioned activities they perform as being before them, giving rise therein to various conceptualizations and false imaginings; it is not that there exists a separate conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).

Thereupon, the Buddha further reflected that these deluded beings remain lost in ignorance; how can they be made to abandon the two selves of person and phenomena, as well as the faults regarding the causes and conditions of agent and action?

Furthermore, he reflects: "How can one awaken to the fact that all conceptual constructions are merely the measure of one's own mind, thereby attaining the transformation of body and mind, ultimately realizing the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*), reaching the realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization, and becoming free from the conceptual constructions regarding the five dharmas and the three natures?"
"Phenomena are but names and signs; seeing them is but delusive thought.
Since you have formed this notion, I therefore say that delusive thought arises from various kinds of false conceptual attachments."

"One who knows the meaning as it truly is" means one who is able to understand the meaning of reality exactly as it is; such a person attains liberation and brings all false conceptualizations to rest.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"All causes and conditions, From these the world arises."
Those who falsely conceptualize and cling to the four extremes do not understand the way I have penetrated reality.
The world is not born from existence, nor is it born from non-existence;
it does not arise from both existence and non-existence, nor from neither existence nor non-existence.
Regarding all causes and conditions, how do the ignorant falsely conceptualize them?
They are neither existent nor non-existent, nor are they both existent and non-existent.
When the Tathāgata contemplates the world, his mind undergoes a transformation and attains non-self.
All natures are unarisen, because they arise from conditions.
All that is produced by conditions is not self-existent;
an entity does not produce itself, for that would entail the fallacy of two entities.
"Because there is no fault in the absence of these two things, no intrinsic nature can be found.
From the beginning of the verse up to "no intrinsic nature can be found," this verse summarizes the faults in the causal conditions previously set forth.

Regarding all causes and conditions: among all worldly phenomena, there are none that do not arise from causes and conditions. Yet, those who harbor false imaginings cling to views of existence, non-existence, and so forth—the four extremes—regarding these causal laws, failing to understand the principle realized by the Tathāgata.

The world does not exist as something produced from birth; it is free from the four extremes of clinging to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), meaning that all phenomena are fundamentally devoid of these four natures.

Furthermore, the passage beginning with "All causes and conditions" continues to refute the aforementioned errors, stating that since all phenomena are fundamentally empty, why do deluded beings give rise to false conceptualizations therein? Not only is there no clinging to the four extremes of existence and non-existence regarding intrinsic nature, but there is also no clinging to the four extremes of appearance regarding non-existence and non-non-existence, as fully detailed in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* concerning the two kinds of emptiness: emptiness of nature and emptiness of characteristics.
If one can observe in this manner, one transforms those two attachments to essence and characteristics and attains the wisdom of the two kinds of selflessness—of persons and phenomena.
However, essence is truly unarisen; it exists because of conditions. Since these phenomena arise from conditions, they lack intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, it is said: "A phenomenon does not give rise to itself. A phenomenon is precisely the fruit; for any dharma that arises, if there is a cause, there must necessarily be a fruit. Just as the cause of karma gives rise to the fruit of birth and death, when one traces the cause back to its origin, since the cause itself is not produced, how could the fruit produce itself?

If there were the faults of either no fruit arising or two fruits arising, one would naturally be free from the clinging to the nature of existence and non-existence; therefore, it is said that "no nature of existence can be apprehended."
"Observing all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), which are free from the grasper (*ālambaka*) and the grasped (*ālambana*);
this mind-only (*cittamātra*) that is no-mind—I call it 'mind-only.
This measure (*māna*) is the locus of intrinsic nature; it is devoid of both conditions (*pratyaya*) and nature (*svabhāva*)."
"The nature is ultimately wondrously pure; I call this 'mind-only' (*cittamātra*).

From this point until the end, these verses praise the aforementioned awakening to the mind-only of one's own deluded thoughts, manifesting the Tathāgata’s realm of self-awakening; these eight lines briefly praise mind-only.
If one does not understand that all phenomena are mind-only, then there will be objects of perception.

When observing with correct wisdom, one becomes detached from both the perceiving mind and the perceived object. Once the subject and object are transcended, there is no mind of discrimination; this is what is meant by "mind-only. Therefore, it is said: "I teach that [all things] are the measure of the mind."

Although one may realize that all phenomena are mind-only, if one still maintains attachment to the nature of objects and has not yet forgotten the thought of the perceiving subject, one must directly transcend both object and nature; only then does it become the ultimate measure of the Tathāgatagarbha-mind.
Regarding "the nature of conditions": "conditions" refers to the subjective perceiver, while "nature" refers to the phenomena that are the objects of perception.
"The conventional self is designated, yet it lacks any substantial reality;
The aggregates are designated as 'aggregates,' and likewise, they lack any substantial reality."
"There are four kinds of equality: that of characteristics, that of the nature of causes, the third, that of non-self and so forth, and the fourth, that of the practice and the practitioner.
Below this, the "mind-measure" (cittamātra) is extensively demonstrated.
The self of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) is the attachment to persons (*pudgala-grāha*).
The aggregates (*skandha*) as aggregates is the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

However, when these two attachments are sought through their specific (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) characteristics, no real entity can be found; thus, all phenomena are equal. Consequently, there are four kinds of views of equality:
If characteristics are identical with the five aggregates, then characteristics and the absence of characteristics are equal;
if characteristics must have causes, then the nature of the cause and the nature of the effect are equal;
because cause and effect are both present, there is a self, and thus the self and non-self are equal.
To be able to realize non-self is cultivation; thus, there is equality between cultivation and non-cultivation.
"When the habitual tendencies of false discrimination are transformed, various kinds of minds arise;
objects manifest externally— this is the conventional mind-measure."
"External manifestations appear but do not exist; the mind perceives their various forms.
Establishing the body and its possessions, I declare this to be the measure of mind (*cittamātra*).

Regarding "delusive conceptualization" and so forth: due to the perfuming of beginningless delusive conceptualization, various consciousnesses arise in succession. Once the deluded mind has been produced, one perceives external objects; this is the conventional measure of mind.

However, external objects fundamentally do not exist; it is due to the mind grasping them that various appearances are perceived. These very five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) constitute the establishment of the body and its possessions; that is to say, the five groups of consciousness and their associated possessions are merely the mental measure of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-citta-mātra*).
"Free from all views, and free from both thought and the object of thought;
neither attainment nor arising—this I call the measure of mind (*cittamātra*).
Neither being nor non-being, it is entirely free from both being and non-being."
That which is called the liberation of the mind, I declare to be the measure of mind (*cittamātra*).
Suchness, the limit of emptiness, nirvāṇa, and the dharma-realm—
these various bodies born of the mind, I declare to be the measure of mind.

The first four lines mean that if one can abandon the views of the two selves—person and phenomena—and abandon both the perceiving subject and the perceived object, then there is neither attainment nor arising; this is the mental measure (*cittamātra*) of right gnosis.
The middle four phrases refer to being free from the fourfold conceptual attachment to the nature of existence and non-existence, as well as being free from the mind that seeks such freedom;

this is precisely the mind-measure (*cittamātra*) of right gnosis (*samyagjñāna*). "Non-nature" means not existent; "non-non-nature" means not non-existent; and "nature and non-nature" refers to both existence and non-existence, as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.

Regarding the latter four phrases: "Suchness" (tathatā) is identical to "True Suchness" (bhūtatathatā); "the limit of emptiness" (śūnyatā-koti) is identical to the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi); "nirvāṇa" is identical to the "ultimate Great Nirvāṇa"; and "Dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu) is identical to the "Buddha-Dharma-realm. These are all different names for a single essence.

By departing from the preceding delusions of names and signs, one reaches right knowledge; through the ultimate *tathatā* and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one abides within the *dharmadhātu* of nirvāṇa. Thus, one is able to manifest various types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) to liberate sentient beings; this is the Tathāgata’s first-principle mind, which is the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*).
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has taught, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should be skilled in words and meanings.”
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful speech and meaning? What is speech? What is meaning?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!”
"Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for your sake.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"Yes, we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "What is speech?"

It refers to the combination of speech, syllables, and conceptual constructions; depending upon the throat, lips, tongue, teeth, gums, and cheeks, it arises from the attachment to the habitual tendencies of the conceptual construction of "I" and "mine" in discourse. This is called speech.

Because the preceding passage mentions terms such as "suchness" (*tathatā*) and "dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*), there arises the inquiry regarding "well-spoken words" (*subhāṣita*) and "well-expounded meaning" (*suartha*).
In the response, the well-spoken words are first clarified, referring to speech, syllables, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and so forth.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"Speech is that which takes the habitual tendencies of discrimination as its cause; it refers to the production of various sounds and the mutual discourse of written characters based upon the throat, tongue, and so forth—this is called speech."
“Mahāmati! What is meant by ‘meaning’ (artha)?
It refers to that which is free from all characteristics of conceptual construction and characteristics of verbal expression; this is called ‘meaning.’”

Mahāmati! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, regarding such meanings as these, dwells alone in a quiet place and, through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, takes as an object the self-realized awakening and heads toward the city of Nirvāṇa; having transformed the body of habitual tendencies, they realize their own enlightened realm and contemplate the characteristics of the superior progress between each stage—this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillfulness in meaning.

Meaning is revealed through words; yet, if one gives rise to views merely following the words, one not only loses the meaning but also becomes confused regarding the names themselves. Therefore, in accordance with the departure from the characteristics of false imagination (*vikalpa*) and the characteristics of verbal expression, it is only through direct realization that one may be said to possess "skillful meaning. Thus, this clarifies the path of cultivation and realization: namely, through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation in a solitary and quiet place, one contemplates and observes the names and meanings as they were heard in relation to the *tathatā* dharma-realm. Taking self-awakened gnosis (*pratyātma-jñāna*) as the object, one proceeds toward *nirvāṇa*, transforms the previously mentioned habitual tendencies of false imagination, and returns to the realm of self-awakening. Practicing the progressive marks of excellence throughout the various stages (*bhūmi*), this is called "skillful meaning."
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Skillful in Speech and Meaning contemplates that speech and meaning are neither different nor not different; he contemplates meaning and speech in the same manner."
If speech were distinct from its meaning, then one would not discern the meaning through speech, but rather enter into the meaning by means of speech, as a lamp illuminates forms.

"Speech" refers to the verbal teachings that express, while "meaning" refers to the principles expressed; this means that one who well understands the expressive reaches the expressed, and one who well understands the expressed realizes the expressive.

Generally speaking from the perspective of the Mahāyāna, although there are the signifier and the signified, the signifier and the signified are non-dual; therefore, it is said that "they are neither different nor not different."

Although meaning may be expressed through false speech, there is no way to discern meaning without speech; thus, one must necessarily enter into meaning by means of speech, just as a lamp illuminates forms.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"For example, it is like a person holding a lamp to illuminate an object, thereby knowing that 'this object is such' and 'it is in such a place. That which is called 'the nature of words is devoid [of inherent existence], which is itself liberation'—is this not what is meant by excellent speech and excellent meaning?"
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!

Regarding such matters as non-arising and non-ceasing, intrinsic nirvāṇa, the three vehicles and the one vehicle, and the self-nature of the mind—if one becomes attached to the meanings of these verbal expressions, one falls into the views of either superimposition or denial."
Based on the construction of difference, various false imaginings arise, appearing as manifold illusions.
Just as with various illusions, ordinary and ignorant sentient beings give rise to false imaginings of difference; this is not the case for the noble ones.
This section speaks of the fault of clinging to words as they are uttered.

For instance, although terms such as "unborn" and "unextinguished" are all merely conventional designations for the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), if one asserts that they truly exist, one falls into the view of eternalism; if one asserts that they truly do not exist, one falls into the view of nihilism—how much more so for other cases?

Regarding the conceptual construction of difference based on difference: this refers to the arising of the clinging to the conceptual construction of difference due to the establishment of distinctions based on verbal expression. It is like seeing a magical illusion and reckoning it as real; such is the vision of the foolish, not that of the noble ones.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Those who engage in the conceptualization of verbal expression establish all phenomena;
because of those establishments, they fall into the hells after death."
Within the aggregates there is no self, nor are the aggregates themselves the self;
it is not as those deluded ones imagine, yet it is also not that there is no self.
All things possess an inherent nature, just as the ignorant and foolish falsely imagine.
If that which is seen by them were real, then everyone should perceive the Truth.
All phenomena lack intrinsic nature; both purity and impurity are entirely non-existent.
They are unreal just as they are perceived, yet they are not nothingness either.
