In the first four phrases, it is stated that the fault of giving rise to views based on words cannot avoid an evil retribution.

It is said that there is no "self" (ātman) within the aggregates (skandhas); this refers to the views of non-Buddhists (tīrthika), which include the notions that there is a self within the aggregates, that the aggregates are within the self, that the aggregates themselves are the self, or that the self is apart from the aggregates.

It is not like those false conceptualizations; that is to say, although it is not like the various attachments to verbal expressions held by the heterodox views of those outsiders—such as [claiming] "there is nothing that is not the self"—[the Tathāgata-garbha is distinct from them].
To claim that all things possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).

If one asserts that all phenomena truly possess an intrinsic nature, one ought to have realized the truths (*satyadarśana*); yet, to speak of an intrinsic nature without having realized the truths is nothing but a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, it is said that to claim all phenomena are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is a view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*); since annihilation implies that neither purity nor defilement exists, this [position] is specifically refuted. The intended meaning is that such a view is no more real than those [other] views previously mentioned.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the characteristics of wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
If you and the other bodhisattvas skillfully discern the characteristics of wisdom and consciousness, you will be able to penetrate their nature and swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Mahāmati! That wisdom is of three kinds: namely, worldly, world-transcending, and world-transcending supreme.
What is worldly wisdom?
This refers to all non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings who cling to the notions of existence and non-existence.
What is supramundane wisdom?
It refers to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who fall into clinging to the expectations regarding individual and common characteristics.
What is the supramundane, most excellent wisdom?

It refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who contemplate all dharmas as non-existent, seeing them as neither arising nor ceasing, and being free from the categories of existence and non-existence; this arises through self-realization within the stage of the Tathāgata, wherein there is the non-self of both persons and phenomena.

In discerning the truth and falsehood of all phenomena and clarifying the right and wrong of words and meanings, nothing surpasses wisdom and consciousness; therefore, the Tathāgata spoke of his own accord without waiting for a question.
However, this wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) have both commonalities and distinctions, as the meaning is evident in the text.
First, it clarifies that there are three kinds of wisdom, which are spoken of in terms of their capacity to know within the mundane and supramundane realms.

Regarding what is called "worldly wisdom" (*loka-jñāna*) by non-Buddhists: generally, those who have left the household life but do not receive the Buddha's teachings are all termed "outsiders. Although the pinnacle of their wisdom may reach as far as the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), their calculations do not transcend existence and non-existence; thus, it is merely called worldly wisdom.

Regarding the statement that within supramundane wisdom the followers of the Two Vehicles fall into the grasping of self-characteristics and common characteristics: because the Two Vehicles contemplate the aggregates, elements, sense bases, causes and conditions, and the Four Noble Truths, they lack the wisdom that transcends both general and specific characteristics; since they loathe birth-and-death and delight in nirvana, it is said that they harbor hopes and cling to them.

Regarding the statement that "supreme wisdom contemplates non-existence," this means that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, employing supreme wisdom, clearly perceive that all dharmas are ultimately empty, fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing, and free from the marks of existence and non-existence. Upon reaching the stage of ultimate enlightenment, there are no longer any distinctions of self or other, nor any marks of form; how then could there be two selves?
This noble wisdom of self-realization is not obtained from without.
"Mahāmati! That which arises and ceases is consciousness; that which neither arises nor ceases is wisdom."

Furthermore, that which falls into the marks of the signless and falls into the various marks of existence and non-existence is consciousness; that which transcends the marks of existence and non-existence is wisdom.
Furthermore, that which nurtures and develops marks is consciousness; that which does not nurture and develop marks is wisdom.
This is a comparative distinction based on the three consciousnesses and the three wisdoms.

It states that phenomena subject to arising and ceasing, which belong to the nine realms, are consciousness; while phenomena free from arising and ceasing, which belong to the Buddha-realm, are wisdom.

Regarding "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "absence of characteristics" (*alakṣaṇa*): "characteristics" refers to existence, while "absence of characteristics" refers to emptiness. This is because the nine realms do not transcend the two extremes of emptiness and existence.
That which falls into emptiness and existence is consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which transcends emptiness and existence is wisdom (*jñāna*).
To speak of "mutual causality" (xiāng yīn) is to do so in relation to the fruit.

To say that "this nourishes consciousness" refers specifically to the context of the non-self of persons and phenomena; it is what was meant in the preceding text by the statement that "form and so forth nourish the mind."

Generally speaking, that which relies upon external objects to nourish what is internal is consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which requires no such dependence and attains its own nature internally is wisdom (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, there are three kinds of wisdom: namely, knowing arising and ceasing, knowing specific and general characteristics, and knowing non-arising and non-ceasing.
Furthermore, the characteristic of non-obstruction is wisdom (*jñāna*), while the characteristic of various obstructed objects is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Furthermore, the characteristic of the means produced by the conjunction of the three factors is consciousness, whereas the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of the means without [external] objects is wisdom.

Furthermore, apprehending characteristics is consciousness (*vijñāna*), while not apprehending characteristics is wisdom (*jñāna*). Because one’s own attainment of the realm of noble wisdom neither emerges nor enters, it is like the moon in water.
These three kinds of wisdom are spoken of in terms of what a single person may know; however, according to the subsequent verse, they are the three kinds known by the Tathāgata.
Knowing arising and ceasing is the knowledge of all (sarvajñatā);
knowing specific and general characteristics is the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā).
To know that which is neither arising nor ceasing is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
It is but a single Buddha-wisdom that possesses three functions, which are termed the "three wisdoms.

Furthermore, it is said that the characteristic of non-obstruction is wisdom; this means that when the aforementioned three wisdoms are fused and merged into a single mind, the absence of any stained or obstructive characteristics is wisdom. Conversely, that which is otherwise is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the three factors are equal," these three factors are the sense organ (*indriya*), the object (*viṣaya*), and the self (*ātman*). Consciousness arises from the conjunction and correspondence of these three factors; it is because this [consciousness] does not know its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*).

If one knows the nature and characteristics [of mind], then the numinous awareness of a single thought-moment does not depend on conditions for its arising; therefore it is said: "The expedient means of non-action, the characteristic of self-nature, is wisdom."

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "attaining the marks and not attaining the marks constitutes wisdom": the "marks" are precisely the marks of the nature-and-phenomena (xingxiang). While the mark is but one, there is a distinction between being detached from it and not being detached; therefore, it is said that they are "attained" or "not attained."

That which is "attained by oneself" refers to the realm of the Tathāgata’s own realized noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), which cannot be designated by names or concepts; therefore, it is said that "it neither emerges nor enters, like the moon in water."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“The accumulation of karma constitutes consciousness; Non-accumulation constitutes wisdom.”
To contemplate all phenomena and realize their non-existence,
thereby attaining the power of mastery— this is what is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
To bind the objects of perception as the mind and for conceptualizations to arise— this is what is called cognition (*jñāna*).
"Non-existence and excellence—wisdom arises from these. Regarding the statement "the accumulation of karma":

"accumulation" (*saṃcaya*) means to gather (*saṃci*) and to assemble (*caya*). Through the faculties encountering their objects, grasping and attachment arise; one initiates wholesome and unwholesome karma and assembles the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). This is what is called consciousness (*vijñāna*).
To be able to comprehend that the faculties and their objects are beyond dependence, such that both self and other are forgotten and no grasping arises—this is called wisdom (*jñāna*).

To observe in this way that phenomena produced by causes and conditions are empty in their very essence, thereby attaining liberation and mastery—this is called the supreme wisdom; here, *prajñā* (insight) is identical to *jñāna* (wisdom).
There are no objects external to the mind; failing to realize that all is but mind, one is turned by objects, which is called bondage.
Mind is precisely consciousness; awakening to this deluded mind constitutes wisdom.
The meaning of the final two lines of the section on "Non-existence" is as seen in the previous explanation:
"Mind, intellect, and consciousness, Far removed from thought and perception,
Attaining the state of non-conceptual dharma— Such are the sons of the Buddha, not the śrāvakas."
The patience of tranquil superior progress, the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom, arises from the excellent ultimate truth; all that is practiced is utterly transcended.
"Mind," "intellect," and "consciousness" are collectively termed "consciousness."
To be far removed from the dharmas of thought is wisdom (*jñāna*).
When one attains the state of non-thought, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are transformed into wisdom.
This belongs to the Bodhisattva and not to the Śrāvaka; this statement marks the beginning of wisdom.
The patience of tranquil superior progress is precisely the Tathāgata’s patience and wisdom of cessation; this refers to the culmination of wisdom.
This pure wisdom arises from the supreme ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and therefore its sphere of activity is entirely free from all attachments.
“I possess three kinds of knowledge, which the Noble Ones have developed as the truth;
by contemplating those perceptions, they fully comprehend all natures.
These are not shared with the two vehicles; this knowledge is free from all that exists.”
"Attachment to intrinsic nature arises from the śrāvakas;
transcending all mental measures, the Tathāgata’s wisdom is pure.

Regarding the three types of wisdom and so forth, these verses clarify that the aforementioned three objects of knowledge are what the Tathāgata has revealed. Thus, although the phenomena of arising and ceasing that constitute the objects of knowledge are all ultimately real, this is what is meant by the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* when it says, "The three wisdoms are one mind."

In that contemplation and so forth, the previous two types of knowledge are reiterated again to manifest the progressively superior wisdom. This means that ordinary beings undergo various states of arising and ceasing due to their false imaginings;

the followers of the Two Vehicles are the opposite of this and thus do not correspond [to reality], for while they are detached from all that exists, they still cling to a self-nature—this is merely the wisdom of the Two Vehicles.
If, however, the Tathāgata’s ultimate wisdom is pure, it transcends all mental measures (*cittamātra*).

"Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are nine kinds of theories of transformation among the non-Buddhists, from which the views of transformation arise. They are: transformation of shape and location, transformation of characteristics, transformation of cause, transformation of accomplishment, transformation of view, transformation of nature, transformation of the clarity of conditions, transformation of the clarity of what is produced, and transformation of things."
Mahāmati! This is called the ninefold view of transformation; it is because of this that all non-Buddhists give rise to theories of existence, non-existence, production, and transformation.
What is the transformation of shape and location?
This refers to the perception of differences in shape and location.
For example, when gold is transformed into various vessels, various shapes and locations appear, yet the nature of the gold does not change; the transformation of all natures is likewise so.

There are some non-Buddhists who harbor such false imaginings, even extending to the false imagination of the transformation of phenomena; these are neither identical nor different, for they are merely false imaginings.

These non-Buddhists falsely calculate nine kinds of theories of transformation—namely, shape, characteristic, cause, and formation—which do not transcend the dharmas of the four great elements and the five aggregates.
Because they perceive the distinct characteristics of arising and ceasing, they postulate the existence of transformation (*pariṇāma*).

However, the True Teaching speaks of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), of being like an illusion (*māyopama*), and of being manifestations of one's own mind; it states that external natures are non-existent and thus unchanging, yet it never definitively asserts [a fixed doctrine]. This is precisely why the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox, and between gain and loss, is established.

"Form" refers to the physical body; "characteristic" refers to the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing; "cause" refers to the cause that produces; "accomplishment" refers to the fruit that is produced; "view" refers to shifting according to external objects; "nature" refers to that which is born again and again without changing; "condition" refers to transformation and cessation due to causes and conditions; "activity" refers to conditioned construction that is not constant; and "phenomenon" refers to conditioned dharmas—these are the nine kinds.

Regarding the statement that "causes give rise to existence and non-existence," this refers to either the non-existence of what previously existed or the existence of what previously did not exist; these are all characteristics of transformation, which do not transcend the realm of existence and non-existence.
The phrase "How so? introduces the interrogation and subsequent explanation.

Regarding "the transformation of form and location": this refers to the physical locations and forms of the four great elements and the sense organs. One perceives these forms changing according to time and thus speaks of "transformation," yet one does not realize that their essential nature never changes.
Gold is transformed into various vessels; although the vessels differ in their many forms, the nature of the gold remains unchanged.

Furthermore, when it is said that "the transformation of all natures is likewise," "nature" refers to the *dharma*. This means that although all *dharmas* undergo transformation, their nature remains unchanged, and this is just so.
There may be non-Buddhists and others who, having formulated their external theories, are here refuted.

To say "that is neither identical nor different" means that they give rise to deluded conceptual discrimination within that which is neither identical nor different; therefore, there are various differences of transformation.
"In this way, one should understand the transformation of all natures.

Just as milk turns into curd, wine ferments, or fruit ripens, so too is the transformation imagined by the non-Buddhists; yet in those cases, there is no actual transformation. Whether existent or non-existent, these are manifestations of one's own mind; external natures have no inherent existence."
Mahāmati! In this way, ordinary and ignorant sentient beings arise from the habitual cultivation of their own false imaginings. Mahāmati!
"There is no dharma that arises or ceases, just as one sees the arising of forms in a dream or an illusion.
Thus, following the section on all natures, he refutes the non-Buddhists' reckoning of the transformation of natures.
First, this is clarified by means of an analogy.

Regarding the phrase "it should be known": those who train in the precepts should know that their conception is like milk, curd, wine, or fruit, which ripen gradually in succession. They perceive it in this way, yet when analyzed through reasoning, it is fundamentally not truly existent; therefore, it is said, "therein is also no transformation."
In fact, all phenomena such as existence and non-existence are manifestations of one's own mind.
Regarding the phrase "external natures are not natures," it means that there are no external objects.
As for the passage beginning with "Thus, ordinary and ignorant [beings]," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"All these arise from the habitual tendencies of one's own discrimination in ignorant and deluded ordinary beings; in reality, not a single dharma is born or ceases. It is like the various forms seen in dreams or illusions, or like speaking of birth and death in relation to the son of a barren woman."

Thus, to not give rise to false views regarding arising and ceasing is the conventional truth; to perceive arising and ceasing and give rise to conceptual attachment is the way of the heterodox; to perceive them as being like dreams and illusions is the penetration of contemplative practice.
To see that all dharmas are manifestations of one’s own mind and to realize that external natures are devoid of intrinsic reality—this is the definitive teaching of this sutra.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Form, location, and time undergo transformation; The four great elements and the various sense faculties...”
The intermediate state arises in succession; such conceptual construction is not the wisdom of the enlightened.
The Supreme One [teaches] dependent origination as not being like that conceptual construction;
yet worldly dependent origination is like a city of the Gandharvas.

The first four lines of the verse describe the erroneous speculations of non-Buddhists regarding transformation; however, these are all merely products of deluded conceptualization and are not the view of the wise.

The latter four lines clarify the Dharma of dependent origination through correct causes and conditions as taught by the Tathāgata; although this differs from those externalist theories, it likewise lacks any real intrinsic nature. Therefore, it is said to be "like a city of the Gandharvas."
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
I pray that you will explain for me the meaning of the continuity of all dharmas and the meaning of liberation."

If one skillfully discriminates the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all phenomena, and if I and the various bodhisattvas are well-versed in the skillful means regarding all continuities, we shall not fall into the conceptual attachment to continuity based on the literal meaning of what has been taught. Being proficient in the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all dharmas, and having awakened from the delusive thoughts of words, letters, and speech, we shall travel through all Buddha-fields, empowered by the seal of the power of immeasurable assemblies, sovereignity, supernormal penetrations, and dharanis. With various transformations and radiant illumination, our awakened wisdom will skillfully enter the ten inexhaustible phrases. Free from expedient practices, like the sun, moon, mani-jewel, and the four great elements, we shall leave behind the self-delusive perceptions of all stages and see all dharmas as being like illusions, dreams, and so forth, thereby entering the body of the Buddha-ground.

Within the realm of all sentient beings, he expounds the Dharma according to their needs and guides them, causing them all to dwell securely in the realization that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams; he leads them away from the categories of existence and non-existence, as well as the conceptual proliferations of arising and ceasing and the divergent meanings of verbal expressions, while his own body becomes increasingly sublime.

When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to enable sentient beings to thoroughly comprehend that all phenomena are fundamentally devoid of the grasping at intrinsic nature, yet they instead give rise to views regarding those verbal expressions, this is called the characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*).
If one realizes that the nature of syllables is devoid of intrinsic reality and that names do not form a continuous succession, this is the characteristic of liberation.
This continuity and non-continuity constitute the very root of saṃsāra and liberation; therefore, Mahāmati requested that this meaning be explained.

"Skillful discernment and so forth" means that if the Tathāgata skillfully discerns these two kinds of characteristics, he will be able to thoroughly understand this Dharma; he will not fall into the continuity of attachment to the characteristics of the literal meaning of what is said, and he will be free from the deluded conceptualization and false discrimination regarding speech and letters—this is precisely what "discernment" (vikalpa) refers to.
Therefore, one is able to universally enter all buddha-fields and advance toward the Way according to each direction.
What are called power, supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), dhāraṇī, and seals (*mudrā*) are precisely the dharma-gates of merit thus attained.

Regarding the various transformations and so forth, it is said that they give rise to transformative functions and emit light that illuminates all things; they skillfully enter the Buddha’s wisdom and fulfill the ten great vows. The "inexhaustible phrases" refer precisely to these vows.

To speak of "practice without expedient means" refers to the absence of deliberate effort; it is like the sun and moon moving through space without any point of attachment, like a mani jewel manifesting according to colors yet lacking inherent nature, and like earth, water, fire, and wind pervading everywhere without obstruction—all these are the characteristics of the Bodhisattva’s transformative path.

Upon traversing the various stages (*bhūmi*), one gradually abandons all delusive thoughts and penetrates the vision that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams. Entering the stage of Buddhahood, one manifests the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*) and universally responds to sentient beings, preaching the Dharma according to their needs to gradually lead them into the ultimate reality.

Furthermore, by realizing that all phenomena are like illusions, one leaves behind views of existence and non-existence, abandons the clinging to arising and ceasing, and does not adhere to verbal expressions; thereafter, as the merit of transformation is attributed to oneself, the characteristics of one's body become increasingly sublime.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well; I shall speak for your sake.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
“Yes, I shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

“There are immeasurable continuities of attachment to the meanings of all dharmas as they are spoken, namely: the continuity of attachment to marks; the continuity of attachment to conditions; the continuity of attachment to existence and non-existence; the continuity of attachment to the false discrimination of arising and non-arising; the continuity of attachment to the false discrimination of cessation and non-cessation; the continuity of attachment to the false discrimination of vehicles and non-vehicles; the continuity of attachment to the false discrimination of the conditioned and the unconditioned; the continuity of attachment to the false discrimination of the specific characteristics of each stage; the continuity of attachment to the uninterrupted false discrimination of one's own [subjective] discrimination; the continuity of attachment to the false discrimination based on the dualistic categories of existence and non-existence held by outsiders; and the continuity of attachment to the uninterrupted false discrimination regarding the three vehicles and the one vehicle.”
In the response, the characteristics of the various continuities (*saṃtāna*) are first demonstrated.

Regarding the phrase "immeasurable," etc., it refers to the ten realms—both the physical environment and its inhabitants, as well as form and mind—from the initial stage of verbal expression to the ultimate state of wordlessness. When one examines the clinging mind, there is virtually nothing that is not a continuity; thus it is said, "clinging to the meaning as it has been explained constitutes a continuity. This refers to what is known as generating understanding in accordance with words.

Among these, the first refers to worldly phenomena: "characteristics" refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), and "conditions" refers to the objective sensory objects (*viṣaya*) that serve as focal points.
"Nature and non-nature" refers to existence and non-existence.
"Arising and non-arising" refers to birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
"Cessation and non-cessation" refers to quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*) and non-quiescent extinction.

"Vehicles and non-vehicles" refers to the internal teachings and external paths; the term "vehicle" (*yāna*) takes the sense of "carrying" as its meaning. Thus, the Great and Small Vehicles can carry one out of birth and death to reach *nirvāṇa*, whereas that which is mounted by external paths cannot carry one out of birth and death; therefore, it is called a "non-vehicle."
The conditioned and the unconditioned refer to mundane and supramundane dharmas, as well as manifest and non-manifest karma.
The "self-characteristics of each stage" refers to the differentiation of the names and characteristics of the various stages.
Regarding the uninterrupted nature of self-conceptualization, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"It is the attachment to what is personally realized through one's own discrimination; this is what is called 'love for dharmas' (*dharmatṛṣṇā*)."
The "Chapter on Existence and Non-existence" is the fundamental basis for the calculations of the non-Buddhists.
"The uninterruptedness of the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle" refers to the absence of any distinction or interruption between the teachings of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!

This and other ordinary, ignorant beings continue in their own false imaginings. Because of this continuity, the false imaginings of the ordinary and ignorant are like a silkworm making a cocoon; by means of the threads of false imagination, they entangle themselves and others, adhering to the marks of the continuity of existence and non-existence."
This "bond" (saṃyojana) rebukes the aforementioned various deluded attachments.

The phrase "this and others" refers to the disciples of our own school, whose attachments are still light; "others" refers to the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), whose attachments are grave. Therefore, it says, "the deluded conceptualizations of the ignorant."

Like a silkworm making its cocoon, one entangles oneself and others with the threads of false conceptualization, unable to emerge from them; in the end, one merely falls into the views of existence and non-existence, or annihilationism and eternalism.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!

Within that state, there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity. Because one perceives all phenomena as quiescent and false conceptualization does not arise, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva perceives all phenomena as quiescent."
Furthermore, Mahāmati!

One awakens to the fact that external natures are neither existent nor non-existent, realizing that the marks manifested by one's own mind are non-existent. By conforming to and observing that all natures—whether existent or non-existent—are merely the manifestations of one's own mind, one perceives the tranquility of the continuity [of consciousness]. Consequently, regarding all phenomena, there is neither the mark of continuity nor the mark of discontinuity.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!

Within that [reality], there is neither bondage nor liberation; it is others who fall into the error of perceiving bondage and liberation because they do not realize things as they truly are. Why is this so?
"This means that regarding all phenomena, existence and non-existence do not exist, because no sentient being can be apprehended.
In this passage, there are three sections.
The phrase "among those" refers to the previously mentioned characteristics of continuity and discontinuity.

This means that one who lacks these two characteristics perceives all phenomena as abiding in tranquility; thus, it is said in the Sūtra: "All phenomena, from the very beginning, are eternally characterized by quiescence."
Furthermore, since all phenomena in the world arise and perish in a continuous flow, how can their quiescence be perceived?

Therefore, it is said that "one awakens to external natures as being without nature," and so forth; this means realizing that all phenomena are mind-only and that there are no phenomena outside the mind. Observing in this way, one naturally perceives that the characteristics of existence and non-existence are entirely empty and quiescent; thus, there are neither characteristics of continuity nor characteristics of non-continuity.

Regarding the statement that there is neither bondage nor liberation: the preceding states of continuity and non-continuity are both termed "bondage," while the wisdom that contemplates quiescence alone is termed "liberation. However, within the reality of suchness (*yathābhūta*), there is fundamentally no bondage or liberation; those who perceive bondage and liberation do so because they fail to see this principle.

Furthermore, he provides an explanatory interpretation, stating that whether all phenomena exist or do not exist, their essential nature cannot be found upon investigation; therefore, it is said that "no sentient beings can be apprehended."
"Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three continuities for the foolish:

namely, greed, hatred, and delusion; as well as craving for future existence accompanied by delight. Because of these continuities, there is the continuity of the realms of existence (*gati*). That continuity continues within the five realms."
Mahāmati! As for the severance of continuity, there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!

When the conditions of the threefold conjunction act as the basis for attachment to expedient means, consciousness arises in uninterrupted succession; through attachment to such expedient means, there is continuity.
When the consciousness of the threefold conjunction ceases and one perceives the three liberations, no further continuity arises.
Greed, hatred, and delusion are the causes of continuity; the five destinies are the fruits of continuity.
From past causes, present fruits are produced; from present actions as causes, future retributions are again summoned.

Regarding the statement "craving for the future," this refers to the craving for desirable retributions in future lives that arises together with delight; because these three poisons continue in succession, there is the revolving through the various realms of existence.
Regarding "destinies" (gati), these refer to the six realms; however, because the asuras are included within the five realms, they are referred to simply as the "five destinies.

Regarding "the severance of continuity," this means that when the three poisons are extinguished, one leaves the five destinies; this is what is meant by the extinction of the cause resulting in the extinction of the effect.

Furthermore, the statement regarding the absence of characteristics of continuity and non-continuity refers to the state of neither bondage nor liberation; that is, the simultaneous vanishing of both object and cognition.

As for the "conditioned harmony of the three," it refers to the false conceptualization of non-Buddhists who reckon that the three conditions—the sense organs, the objects, and the self—harmonize, whereby the various consciousnesses arise in successive continuity.
Furthermore, regarding what is called "clinging to expedient means": if there is attachment, then the continuity [of afflictions] will be uninterrupted;
if one understands the three conditions, abandons all attachments, and perceives the three kinds of liberation, then this continuity will not arise.

The three liberations are: liberation through intrinsic purity, liberation through perfect purity, and liberation through the purity of skillful means. Indeed, the realization of the three conditions is itself the three liberations; they do not exist separately from them.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Unreal conceptualization—this is called the characteristic of continuity.
If one knows that reality, the net of continuity is severed."
Lacking knowledge of all natures, they grasp at them according to verbal designations;
like silkworms that spin a web to entangle themselves,
the deluded are bound by their own false imaginings and fail to observe the continuity [of existence].
This verse merely concerns whether the preceding [state] continues or does not continue, and whether it is true or false; that which is false continues, while that which is true does not continue.
If one realizes that the false is itself the true, then all phenomena are of one suchness—how could there be continuity or non-continuity?

If one lacks knowledge regarding all phenomena and clings to them according to mere words, one will bind oneself and others like a silkworm spinning its cocoon, without interruption, due to a failure to investigate.
On the contrary, when one contemplates this, how can there be any continuity?
